title: Matot: clear before all (Numbers 32:22)
hookLine: be "clear before the LORD, and before Israel": innocent, and seen to be fair

cards: The treasurer of the parents' association suddenly has a new car. Maybe it was an inheritance. Maybe a raise.
It's probably fine. But people talk, and once they start, it's hard to stop them. Being honest and looking honest aren't quite the same thing.
Moses knew it. As he finishes the deal with Reuben and Gad, he adds a phrase that sounds like legal fine print. The rabbis turned it into a very practical rule for daily life.

teach.h: NEKIYIM: CLEAR BEFORE GOD AND ISRAEL.
teach.b: Moses tells the two tribes: if you cross over and fight until the land is subdued, and then come back, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, "ye shall be clear before the LORD, and before Israel."
Clear before God, and also before the people. In Hebrew, nekiyim: clean, innocent. It isn't enough that God knows you kept your promise.
The other tribes have to be able to see it too. The rabbis built a whole way of living on that phrase, and before Israel.

teach.h: NO HEM, NO POCKET, NO SHOES.
teach.b: In the Mishnah, tractate Shekalim, the person who went into the Temple treasury chamber to take out coins couldn't wear a garment with a hem, or shoes, or tefillin, or an amulet. Anywhere a coin might hide. Why?
In case he became poor, people would say it was punishment for stealing; in case he became rich, they'd say he took it from the chamber.
Then the Mishnah quotes this verse: a person must be clear before people, just as before God. The Talmud tells of two priestly families with secret skills.
One baked the special bread for the Temple; its children were never seen eating fine bread, so no one could suspect the family of taking any.

The other made the Temple incense; its brides never wore perfume, for the same reason. That's a lot to give up, so that their honesty would be visible, not just real. The point isn't image management.
Trust is something the whole community shares, and you protect it by leaving nothing to suspect.

how: The principle drawn from Numbers 32:22, being clear before people as before God, guides Jewish practice in handling communal funds, and the Mishnah's rules for the Temple treasury are still taught as its classic example.

games.q: what's inside the rule — tap the pairs.

s: the Torah says it's enough to be honest before God alone
clear before the LORD, and before Israel: people have to be able to see it too.
the Temple treasury collector wore no garment where coins could hide
Mishnah Shekalim says no hem, no shoes, no tefillin, no amulet.
the rule is mainly about protecting your image

games.q: you're chosen to collect coins from the Temple treasury chamber. how do you dress?
o: in your best robe, with deep pockets.
with no hem, no pockets, no shoes.
games.why: the Mishnah says nothing that could hide a coin, so that whether you grow rich or poor, nobody could suspect you.

practice: Think of something in your life that's perfectly fine but might look odd from outside: money you handle for others, a decision you made quietly, a friendship someone might misread.
Ask whether saying it out loud would make it clearer, not out of guilt, but to keep trust easy.
